A baseload plant may produce 5000 MW constantly... but somewhere in the system is a peaker plant that DOES adjust its output as demand fluctuates. They're mostly natural gas combustion turbines or hydro now, although wind turbines can and are used as well, because that 5000MW plant takes hours to adjust its output. 

When you turn on the lights, the amount of power in the system doesn't change initially... but get shared between more users. This manifests as a very slight drop in system voltage, which dims your neighbours lights fractionally. Back at the power plant, the voltage drop makes the generator harder to turn, increasing the amount of steam needed to maintain constant rotation speed, dropping the pressure in the boiler. Thus, the burners are turned up slightly to increase steam output... bringing everything back up to nominal parameters   Thus, turning on the light DOES impact fuel usage ultimately.

REITs reported earnings are distorted by CCA (depreciation) which is deducted when calculating reported earnings even though it is a non-cash expense and typically a chunk or all of it is flowed through to unit holders in their distributions (that is why REITs typically have a large ROC (return of capital) component in their distributions).
